## AI-generated Overview (from reference literature and SuttaCentral)
*This overview was drafted by an AI model from the cited scholarship and SuttaCentral data and may contain errors; verify against the sources before relying on it.*
The *Ulūkajātaka* (Ja 270), titled "The Owl", is a narrative included in the *Kosiyavagga* of the Pali Jātaka collection [SuttaCentral; Fausböll 1879]. According to the frame story, the Buddha delivered this discourse while residing at Jetavana to address a recurring conflict between crows and owls (*kākolūkakalaha*) [SuttaCentral; Fausböll 1879]. In the story of the past, the birds assemble in the Himalayas to elect a sovereign ruler; although they initially intend to crown the owl, a crow vigorously objects, prompting the assembly to instead select a golden goose (*suvaṇṇahaṁsa*) as their king [Tambiah 1976; Fausböll 1879]. In the identification of the birth story, the Buddha identifies himself as the young goose prince who was inaugurated as monarch [Tambiah 1976; Fausböll 1879].
In early Buddhist material culture, scenes representing the *Ulūkajātaka* are depicted in relief among ancient Mathurā sculptures alongside several other classic Jātaka tales [Chauley 1998]. Sociological and anthropological studies highlight the story as an archetype of righteous animal kingship elected through collective consensus [Tambiah 1976].
SuttaCentral records four translations across four languages and lists no early canonical parallels in other languages [SuttaCentral]. DharmaNexus detects Pali-internal text reuse across seven matching passages (amounting to 465 characters) with the *Jātaka-aṭṭhakathā* (Dutiyo bhāgo), with its longest segment alignment at §2.1–2.4 corresponding to commentary §2290–2293 (similarity 0.95); no cross-language text reuse matches are recorded above threshold [DharmaNexus].
